cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Federal buyers, the FDA, and the EU’s CRA era all want your software’s ingredients list and next year’s CVE will interrogate the SBOMs you generate today.

Evaluating these platforms alongside the Top 10 Best Software Supply Chain Security Tools shows that simply creating a static inventory is insufficient; organizations must manage, correlate, and monitor those inventories across the entire development lifecycle.

We scored ten options across generation, management, and monitoring, with a status flag where the roster demanded honesty.

Anchore’s Syft takes 1 as the free generation standard; FOSSA and Cybeats complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Syft the generator the ecosystem standardized on, free.

• Podium: Syft (generation), FOSSA (license+SBOM workflows), Cybeats (lifecycle monitoring).

• Regulated depth: Finite State extracts SBOMs from firmware binaries the device-mandate lane.

• Status honesty: Rezilion’s wind-down makes it a cautionary flag, not a pick.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: format fidelity (CycloneDX/SPDX), transitive depth, VEX support, monitoring capability, regulatory fit, pricing transparency, status currency.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: lane fit 25%, format/VEX depth 25%, monitoring 20%, pricing clarity 15%, regulatory alignment 15%.

The 2026 SBOM Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores. n/r = not rated pending status.

1. Anchore (Syft) — Best Free Generation

Snapshot: OSS free + enterprise | Images/filesystems/archives | Both formats

Why it earns 1: The generator everyone standardized on: accurate, fast, native to both CycloneDX and SPDX, and built for CI pipelines.

Operating alongside the Top 10 Best Container Image Scanning Tools, Syft pairs with Grype for vulnerability scanning and Anchore Enterprise for centralized policy enforcement.

Standout features: Multi-target generation; format fidelity; Grype pairing; CI-native.

Pros: Free; ubiquitous; accurate.

Cons: Management/monitoring upstack.

Bottom line: Emit SBOMs from every build, starting today, free.

2. FOSSA — Best Management Workflows

Snapshot: Free tier + tiers | License + SBOM unified | Attribution automation

Why it earns 2: SBOMs meet the legal obligations they exist for: corporate license policy, automated attribution notices, and export workflows that legal counsel can sign off on.

Grounded in Software Composition Analysis (SCA) and license compliance policies, FOSSA combines open-source governance with vulnerability management into a single workflow.

Standout features: SBOM export; license policy; attribution; vuln overlay.

Pros: Workflow depth; free entry.

Cons: Firmware lane elsewhere.

Bottom line: The SBOM your lawyers co-own.

3. Cybeats — Best Lifecycle Monitoring

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | SBOM Studio | Continuous CVE mapping

Why it earns 3: Generation is only day one; Cybeats watches the shelf. SBOM Studio continuously maps newly disclosed CVEs against historical inventories without requiring code rescans.

It acts as an operational layer for continuous vulnerability management and exposure tracking, enabling VEX generation and secure customer-facing sharing portals.

Standout features: Ingestion/scoring; continuous monitoring; VEX; sharing portal.

Pros: Lifecycle focus.

Cons: Pair with generation.

Bottom line: The SBOM shelf that watches itself.

4. Finite State — Best Embedded/Firmware Depth

Snapshot: Quote | Binary-composition analysis | Device mandates

Why it earns 4: FDA-class medical device mandates and industrial standards meet upstream suppliers who refuse to share source code.

Finite State extracts SBOMs directly from compiled firmware binaries, addressing the challenges of embedded systems security and firmware validation by correlating hardware and binary components with known vulnerabilities.

Standout features: Binary analysis; firmware SBOMs; device correlation; compliance reporting.

Pros: Regulated-device fit.

Cons: Device-lane scope.

Bottom line: Ingredients lists from binaries alone.

5. Manifest — Best Supplier-SBOM Ingestion

Snapshot: Tiered | Ingest/normalize/monitor | Federal traction

Why it earns 5: The third-party consumption problem solved: collecting, normalizing, and continuously monitoring the disparate SBOMs your enterprise suppliers deliver.

It acts as an operational bridge for supply chain intelligence and third-party risk analysis, turning supplier PDFs and disconnected JSON files into searchable inventories.

Standout features: Ingestion at scale; normalization; monitoring; sharing.

Pros: Consumption depth.

Cons: Young vendor.

Bottom line: Makes supplier SBOMs mean something.

6. Snyk — Best Dev-Flow Generation

Snapshot: Free + per-dev | Export from existing scans

Why it earns 6: SBOM generation delivered as a natural byproduct of security scanning already active across developer repositories.

Leveraging Snyk’s dependency graph, engineering teams can export CycloneDX and SPDX documents while benefiting from AI-assisted automated remediation and fix pull requests to resolve discovered vulnerabilities before shipping.

Standout features: SBOM export; platform unity; API.

Pros: Zero-new-tool path.

Cons: Management elsewhere.

Bottom line: The export hiding in your current subscription.

7. Sonatype — Best Policy-Tied Platform

Snapshot: Tiered | Lifecycle + Firewall enforcement

Why it earns 7: Ingredients lists directly tied to ingestion policy: generating the SBOM that actively blocks risky components at the door.

Backed by Sonatype Nexus Repository security advisories and Nexus Lifecycle, it prevents malicious or non-compliant dependencies from entering builds.

Standout features: SBOM generation; policy tie; research data.

Pros: Enforcement link.

Cons: Nexus gravity.

Bottom line: The inventory with a bouncer attached.

8. JFrog — Best Registry-Native

Snapshot: Platform tiers | Build-info lineage | Xray-correlated

Why it earns 8: SBOMs generated where binary artifacts live: using Artifactory build-info as the immutable single source of truth.

As organizations track active JFrog Artifactory enterprise security updates, JFrog Xray correlates vulnerabilities and cryptographically signed release bundles directly from the registry.

Standout features: Build-info SBOMs; Xray tie; distribution.

Pros: Source-of-truth fit.

Cons: Platform gravity.

Bottom line: The registry writing its own receipts.

9. Mend — Best Automation-Linked

Snapshot: Tiered | Renovate-connected bills

Why it earns 9: The software inventory that automatically schedules its own updates: connecting SBOM component tracking directly to automated remediation workflows.

Mend couples inventory export with automating dependency updates across CI/CD pipelines, turning outdated components into tracked pull requests.

Standout features: SBOM export; automation tie; compliance.

Pros: Fix-path link.

Cons: Lifecycle depth elsewhere.

Bottom line: From ingredients list to update queue.

10. sbomify — Best SBOM Lifecycle & Sharing Platform

Snapshot: Free + paid tiers | SBOM lifecycle management | VEX + sharing workflows

Why it earns 10: sbomify turns SBOMs into living security artifacts by combining generation, management, vulnerability tracking, VEX, and controlled sharing in one workflow.

Standout features: CycloneDX/SPDX support; VEX; vulnerability monitoring; SBOM sharing; CI/CD integrations.

Pros: Strong lifecycle coverage; free entry; good compliance and sharing workflows.

Cons: Smaller ecosystem and market footprint than larger enterprise platforms.

Bottom line: From SBOM generation to continuous sharing and compliance in one platform.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Generate Free, Then Buy Your Obligation

Syft in CI this week costs nothing and future-proofs every build. Then buy the lane your obligations name: legal workflows (FOSSA), portfolio monitoring (Cybeats), supplier ingestion (Manifest), firmware mandates (Finite State) or export from platforms you already run (Snyk/Sonatype/JFrog).

Attach VEX so ingested bills don’t scream on every CVE, and retire wound-down vendors from shortlists before procurement does.

FAQs

What is the best SBOM tool in 2026? Anchore’s Syft ranks 1 for free generation, FOSSA for license-integrated management, Cybeats for lifecycle monitoring with Finite State owning firmware mandates and Manifest the supplier-ingestion lane.

What regulations demand SBOMs? US federal procurement (EO 14028 lineage), FDA premarket device cybersecurity, and the EU Cyber Resilience Act era plus enterprise contracts citing all three. Generation is table stakes; monitoring makes it real.

CycloneDX or SPDX? Support both serious tools do. CycloneDX (OWASP) leads security use cases and VEX; SPDX (Linux Foundation) leads license heritage. The format war matters less than emitting consistently.

What is VEX and why does it matter? Exploitability statements accompanying SBOMs declaring which component CVEs actually affect the product. Without VEX, every ingested bill looks on fire; with it, triage breathes.

What happened to Rezilion? The runtime-SBOM pioneer wound down a reminder that this young market’s vendors need stability checks alongside feature comparisons.

How do SBOM tools integrate with artifact storage? Modern solutions integrate directly with container registry security tools and artifact managers, storing SBOMs alongside container digests and binary packages as tamper-evident metadata.

Verdict

Syft floors generation free, FOSSA and Cybeats make bills live, and the mandate lanes (Finite State, Manifest) serve the regulators arriving fastest emit today, monitor tomorrow, attach VEX always, and check every vendor’s pulse in a market young enough to bury pioneers.

Maintaining cryptographically verifiable software bills of materials provides the foundational transparency required to uphold an authentic Zero Trust security architecture. Emit inventories from every build, monitor them over time, accompany them with VEX statements, and choose vendors with proven operational stability.

The 2026 CI/CD Security Power Rankings

While organizations must manage risks highlighted by GitHub Actions supply chain vulnerabilities and runner token exposures, GHAS establishes the baseline every dedicated tool must justify displacing.

Standout features: Push protection; CodeQL; Actions policies; artifact attestation; dependency review.

Pros: Native; per-committer pricing.

Cons: GitHub-scoped; runner hardening thin (see 4).

Bottom line: Activate before any dedicated RFP.

2. Cycode — Best VCS-to-Pipeline Graph

Snapshot: Quote | Native engines + risk graph | Source-control roots

Why it earns 2: Code, secrets, and pipeline posture connected in one graph the dedicated platform whose roots (VCS and pipeline security) match where attacks moved.

Backed by threat intelligence like Cycode research uncovering authentication and SDK vulnerabilities, it correlates developer identities with workflow permissions.

Standout features: Pipeline posture; secrets; hardening; risk graph.

Pros: Breadth + graph.

Cons: Quote-based.

Bottom line: The factory and its code, one lens.

3. Legit Security — Best Factory Integrity

Snapshot: Quote | Discovery + tamper detection

Why it earns 3: You can’t defend pipelines you can’t name Legit inventories the build estate, watches for tampering, and scores SDLC posture. The SolarWinds lesson, productized.

It defends against incidents like supply-chain attacks targeting build environments and forged pipeline provenance by monitoring the systems that compile application code.

Standout features: Pipeline discovery; integrity monitoring; misconfig governance.

Pros: Integrity depth.

Cons: Pair for code-side scope.

Bottom line: Knows every workflow that can reach production.

4. StepSecurity — Best Runner Hardening

Snapshot: Free + published tiers | Harden-Runner egress control

Why it earns 4: The attack that actually happens malicious dependencies exfiltrating from CI dies at egress control. Action pinning and runner policies close the layer natives leave open, free tier included.

StepSecurity provides actionable defense against campaigns like the GhostAction supply chain campaign that abuses GitHub Actions to steal CI/CD credentials, blocking outbound exfiltration at the operating system layer.

Standout features: Harden-Runner; egress filtering; action pinning; policies.

Pros: Attack-relevant niche; free floor.

Cons: Actions-scoped.

Bottom line: The runner that can’t phone home to attackers.

5. GitLab — Best Single-Platform DevSecOps

Snapshot: Published tiers | Ultimate security suite

Why it earns 5: Scanning, compliance pipelines, and protected environments as platform features one product decision covering the SDLC for GitLab estates.

Despite requiring operational diligence around critical GitLab CI/CD vulnerabilities and API security updates, GitLab Ultimate delivers exceptional end-to-end coherence.

Standout features: Built-in scanners; compliance frameworks; protected envs.

Pros: Coherence; published pricing.

Cons: Depth vs specialists.

Bottom line: The all-in-one answer for its own estate.

6. Arnica — Best Behavioral Defense

Snapshot: Published tiers | Anomalous-dev detection | ChatOps fixes

Why it earns 6: Pipelines fail through people and permissions Arnica watches for anomalous pushes and excess rights, fixing via chat at published rates.

It pairs behavioral tracking with developer-first static code analysis and posture checks to automate real-time remediation directly within Slack and Microsoft Teams.

Standout features: Behavioral detection; permission rightsizing; secrets; ChatOps.

Pros: Behavior lens; pricing clarity.

Cons: Younger ecosystem.

Bottom line: Notices the commit that isn’t like the others.

7. OX Security — Best PBOM Traceability

Snapshot: Tiered | Commit-to-workload lineage | Enforcement options

Why it earns 7: Provides every build artifact with an immutable biography: tracking which commit produced it, which pipeline compiled it, and which production cluster runs it.

Backed by security research including OX Security vulnerability research uncovering command execution flaws, its Pipeline Bill of Materials (PBOM) gives security teams automated enforcement policies that block unverified builds.

Standout features: PBOM; code-to-cloud mapping; native scans; enforcement.

Pros: Lineage clarity.

Cons: Scale checks.

Bottom line: Provenance with teeth.

8. Apiiro — Best Risk-Graph Context

Snapshot: Quote | Material-change detection

Why it earns 8: Highlights which specific pipeline or code change actually altered your organization’s risk profile.

Utilizing AI-driven application risk-graph visualization and deep architecture mapping, Apiiro monitors code changes from initial pull request through build and deployment, identifying risky material changes to authorization boundaries.

Standout features: Risk graph; change detection; SDLC posture.

Pros: Context depth.

Cons: Maturity assumed.

Bottom line: Knows which change mattered.

9. Aqua (Argon) — Best CNAPP-Absorbed Lane

Snapshot: Tiered | Argon inside since 2021

Why it earns 9: Pipeline security delivered within a broader cloud-native application protection platform.

Integrating Argon Security’s technology, it protects software supply chain pipelines even as threat actors launch supply chain attacks targeting open-source scanners and tools, connecting build integrity checks directly to container admission controllers.

Standout features: Pipeline scanning; posture; CNAPP unity.

Pros: Platform path.

Cons: Standalone momentum.

Bottom line: Factory security in the container estate.

10. Palo Alto (Cider) — Best Prisma-Absorbed Lane

Snapshot: Quote | Cider inside since 2023

Why it earns 10: Pipeline security and posture management integrated directly into Prisma Cloud’s code-to-cloud security architecture.

Incorporating Cider Security’s pipeline research, it protects environments where threat actors leverage CI/CD environments to compromise cloud resources, tying misconfigured GitHub Actions directly to production IAM roles.

Standout features: Pipeline inventory; posture; CNAPP context.

Pros: Cloud-context tie.

Cons: Packaging shifts.

Bottom line: Pipeline risk in the platform ledger.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Activate, Harden, Discover

Native controls first GHAS or GitLab Ultimate reset every case. Harden the execution layer next (StepSecurity-class pinning and egress this week, it’s cheap).

Then buy discovery and integrity (Cycode/Legit) when workflows outnumber memory, behavior watching (Arnica) where dev-account risk matters, and evaluate absorbed lanes (Argon/Cider) through their parent platforms. Attestation is a build output now treat it that way.

FAQs

What is the best CI/CD security tool in 2026? GitHub Advanced Security ranks 1 as the native floor most estates should activate, Cycode and Legit lead dedicated posture and integrity, StepSecurity owns runner hardening with GitLab’s platform lane and the absorbed options (Argon/Aqua, Cider/Palo Alto) serving their estates.

What attacks does pipeline security stop? Poisoned pipelines, malicious dependencies executing in CI, runner exfiltration, tampered builds, and stolen deploy credentials the tradecraft behind the decade’s worst supply-chain incidents.

Where do we start this week? Push protection on, actions pinned, runner egress filtered free-to-cheap moves that close the paths attackers actually use. Discovery follows when you can’t name every workflow with production reach.

How does CI/CD pipeline security connect to Application Security Posture Management (ASPM)? Pipeline security governs the integrity of the build factory, while Application Security Posture Management (ASPM) platforms aggregate, deduplicate, and prioritize the vulnerabilities discovered across all scanners running within those pipelines.

What happened to Argon and Cider? Acquired into Aqua (2021) and Palo Alto (2023) respectively both sell inside platforms now; evaluate current packaging.

Native controls or dedicated platforms? Natives first, always then dedicated lanes for what they miss: cross-platform discovery, integrity monitoring, behavioral detection, and runner-layer hardening.

Verdict

GitHub proves the factory can guard itself, Cycode and Legit map what sprawls beyond it, and StepSecurity locks the door attackers actually use activate, harden, discover, in that order, and let attestations flow from every build. The pipeline is the crown jewel now; fund it like one.

articles.title: Top 10 Best RASP Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:
RASP’s idea block attacks from inside the running app won so convincingly that observability and edge platforms absorbed it, leaving a thinner standalone market that stale lists misrepresent. Rather than relying solely on pre-deployment scans from static application security testing (SAST) tools, modern engineering organizations deploy real-time runtime protection directly inside running workloads to intercept […]

The post Top 10 Best RASP Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
RASP’s idea block attacks from inside the running app won so convincingly that observability and edge platforms absorbed it, leaving a thinner standalone market that stale lists misrepresent.

Rather than relying solely on pre-deployment scans from static application security testing (SAST) tools, modern engineering organizations deploy real-time runtime protection directly inside running workloads to intercept memory corruption, command injections, and zero-day execution paths.

Our roster resolves to nine real entries (Hdiv sells inside Datadog since 2022; K2 Cyber carries a defunct-status flag). Contrast Security takes 1; Datadog and Waratek complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Contrast Protect the dedicated standard-bearer, testing-to-production on one agent.

• Podium: Contrast (dedicated), Datadog (Hdiv’s engine at APM reach), Waratek (JVM virtual patching).

• Check your toggles: Dynatrace and Datadog estates may already own runtime blocking unactivated.

• Different job alert: Jscrambler protects the browser side client-side shielding, budgeted separately.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: protection depth, overhead reputation, deployment model, consolidation accuracy, pricing transparency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: in-process depth 30%, deployment burden 25%, platform economics 20%, status honesty 15%, ecosystem 10%.

The 2026 RASP Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores. n/r = not rated pending status.

1. Contrast Security — Best Dedicated RASP

Snapshot: Per-app/quote | Protect + Assess continuity | Broad language agents

Why it earns 1: The company that bet on instrumentation executes production protection deepest exploit blocking with code-level context, from the same agents that verified in testing.

It provides native Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST) continuity while reinforcing secure coding practices and remediation workflows across development teams.

Standout features: In-app blocking; attack visibility; IAST continuity; language breadth.

Pros: Depth; one-agent story.

Cons: Agent lifecycle; per-app economics.

Bottom line: The pure dedicated play, still standing tallest.

2. Datadog (incl. Hdiv) — Best APM-Delivered

Snapshot: Published usage | Hdiv engine inside | Zero new agents

Why it earns 2: Runtime protection delivered as a toggle on tracing agents already running across your fleet.

Powered by Hdiv’s acquired technology, Datadog leverages its presence among top Application Performance Monitoring (APM) tools to deliver in-app protection with transparent usage-based billing.

Standout features: Exploit blocking; trace-context evidence; APM unity.

Pros: Deployment-free; pricing clarity.

Cons: Dedicated-depth contests.

Bottom line: RASP at the reach of the agent you already run.

3. Waratek — Best JVM Virtual Patching

Snapshot: Quote | Patch without redeploying | Legacy Java’s shield

Why it earns 3: JVM-level rules neutralize vulnerable application behavior without requiring source code modifications serving as the definitive virtual patching solution for Log4j-class emergency vulnerabilities inside legacy enterprise Java stacks that cannot ship rapid updates.

Standout features: Virtual patching; JVM instrumentation; legacy support.

Pros: Patch-without-deploy.

Cons: JVM scope.

Bottom line: The emergency fix that skips the release train.

4. Dynatrace — Best OneAgent Defense

Snapshot: Published usage | Detect-and-block on OneAgent

Why it earns 4: Application Security rides instrumentation Dynatrace estates already deploy exposure-ranked, Davis-prioritized, and activated with a switch.

It injects runtime application self-protection (RASP) rules directly into execution flows to halt injection attempts without external appliances.

Standout features: OneAgent delivery; runtime blocking; exposure ranking.

Pros: Zero-new-agent; usage pricing.

Cons: Platform gravity.

Bottom line: Check this toggle before any RASP RFP.

5. Fastly (Signal Sciences) — Best Edge-Adjacent

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | NGWAF at runtime’s job

Why it earns 5: The Next-Gen WAF that absorbed much of the market demand originally aimed at RASP.

Recognized across enterprise Web Application Firewall (WAF) solutions, Signal Sciences delivers app-aware blocking as a web server module, container sidecar, or edge proxy without invasive in-process code instrumentation.

Standout features: NGWAF; flexible deployment; app-aware rules.

Pros: Pragmatism; developer goodwill.

Cons: Not in-process context.

Bottom line: Why many teams never bought classic RASP.

6. Imperva — Best WAAP-Estate Pairing

Snapshot: Quote | Thales family | Defense-in-depth

Why it earns 6: In-app execution depth positioned behind the perimeter gateway you have tuned for years.

Imperva delivers RASP protection as an integrated defense layer within its modern WAAP portfolio, shielding backend services from attacks that slip past edge heuristics.

Standout features: RASP module; WAAP unity; virtual patching support.

Pros: Estate synergy.

Cons: Standalone momentum.

Bottom line: The layered pick for Imperva estates.

7. Jscrambler — Best Client-Side Lane

Snapshot: Tiered | Browser-side shielding | PCI 6.4.3 tailwind

Why it earns 7 (as its own job): A fundamentally different battlefield: JavaScript code obfuscation, anti-tampering, and skimming defense against Magecart attacks executing within untrusted end-user browsers.

It brings RASP’s defensive principles directly to modern e-commerce checkout environments.

Standout features: JS protection; anti-tamper; skimming detection; PCI-aligned monitoring.

Pros: Owns its lane; regulatory push.

Cons: Not server-side RASP budget separately.

Bottom line: The checkout page’s bodyguard.

8. OpenText (Fortify) — Best Suite-Governed

Snapshot: Quote | SSC integration | On-prem capable

Why it earns 8: Runtime protection managed under sovereign-friendly governance for Fortify-standardized estates.

Fortify delivers in-process shielding alongside runtime vulnerability testing across live web applications and dynamic application security testing (DAST) platforms to satisfy air-gapped compliance mandates.

Standout features: Runtime agents; SSC unity; policy.

Pros: Governance continuity.

Cons: Category momentum.

Bottom line: In-app defense inside the compliance plane.

9. Oligo Security — Best ADR / Runtime Exploit Defense

Snapshot: Commercial | Runtime visibility | Exploit detection and blocking

Why it earns 9: Oligo brings modern application detection and response (ADR) and runtime threat detection to production environments, using runtime behavior and deep application context to identify exploitable risks and active attacks backed by threat intelligence from Oligo Security researchers uncovering critical runtime RCE vulnerabilities.

Standout features: Runtime exploit detection; behavioral context; exploitability prioritization; runtime blocking; application visibility.

Pros: Modern runtime-security approach; strong production context.

Cons: More ADR-focused than traditional in-process RASP.

Bottom line: Modern runtime defense built around what applications actually execute.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Toggles First, Depth Where It Counts

Audit your APM’s security switches before any RFP Datadog/Dynatrace estates often own the capability unactivated.

Buy dedicated (Contrast) where in-process context is the requirement, Waratek where Java can’t redeploy, Jscrambler where the browser is the battlefield and prune dead names (K2) plus absorbed ones (Hdiv) from shortlists before procurement embarrasses itself.

Deployment realism decides outcomes here more than feature matrices. Start runtime protection in monitor-only mode on one tier-one app, measure overhead and false-block rates against real traffic for a sprint, then graduate to blocking on the routes where evidence supports it teams that flip global blocking on day one usually flip it off by day ten.

Pair every in-process layer with your WAAP rather than replacing it: the edge absorbs volumetric noise cheaply, leaving the agent to judge the requests that deserve code-level scrutiny.

And budget the client side separately PCI DSS 6.4.3-era requirements make payment-page script defense (Jscrambler-class) a compliance line item now, not an optional extra.

Common Pitfalls

Global blocking enabled before monitor-mode evidence; RASP purchased while the APM’s included protection sits dark; client-side and server-side lanes confused in one budget; dead vendors surviving on shortlists; and agents deployed without platform-engineering ownership of overhead.

FAQs

What is the best RASP tool in 2026? Contrast Protect ranks 1 for dedicated in-process protection, Datadog (Hdiv’s engine inside) for APM-delivered blocking, Waratek for JVM virtual patching with Dynatrace toggles, Fastly’s edge lane, and Jscrambler’s client-side job rounding the field.

Is RASP dead as a category? The capability thrives; the standalone market thinned. Platforms absorbed the demand our nine-entry honest count (with one defunct flag) tells the story stale lists don’t.

What happened to Hdiv and K2? Hdiv was acquired by Datadog (2022) and powers its runtime protection; K2’s signals point to wind-down verify before any consideration.

How does RASP interact with a Web Application Firewall (WAF)? They operate at different layers: WAAP gateways inspect perimeter traffic at the CDN edge, while RASP evaluates execution context inside the runtime environment.

Even when vulnerabilities affect edge WAF and CDN architectures, in-process RASP agents intercept the underlying malicious payload before execution.

RASP vs WAF both? Different vantage: WAAP filters broadly at the edge; RASP blocks with code context in-process. Common pattern: WAAP everywhere, in-process depth on crown jewels.

What about client-side protection? A distinct job script integrity and skimming defense (Jscrambler-class), now PCI-driven for payment pages. Budget it separately from server RASP.

Verdict

Contrast keeps the dedicated crown, Datadog proves distribution wins, and Waratek owns the emergency-patch niche activate what your agents already can, buy depth where context demands, and let the dead names rest. Nine entries, honestly counted; one idea, thoroughly absorbed.

articles.title: Meta Zurp AI Toolkit Connects Burp Suite With AI Coding Agents for Bug Bounty Research
articles.description:
Meta has introduced Zurp, an open-source toolkit that connects Burp Suite workflows with AI coding agents for approved bug bounty research. The project is designed for vetted researchers in Meta’s bug bounty program and brings several research functions into one place, reducing the need to switch between separate tools, logins, and tokens while testing Meta-owned […]

The post Meta Zurp AI Toolkit Connects Burp Suite With AI Coding Agents for Bug Bounty Research appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Meta has introduced Zurp, an open-source toolkit that connects Burp Suite workflows with AI coding agents for approved bug bounty research.

The project is designed for vetted researchers in Meta’s bug bounty program and brings several research functions into one place, reducing the need to switch between separate tools, logins, and tokens while testing Meta-owned targets.

Zurp works as a Java extension inside Burp Suite and also offers Model Context Protocol, or MCP, servers for AI agents. This design lets a researcher inspect web traffic in Burp Suite while using the same approved Meta APIs and access token through an AI coding assistant.

The tool is intended only for data and test assets linked to the researcher’s own authorized account, which is an important boundary for safe and legal security testing.

At the center of the project is the Meta View tab. It helps researchers understand identifiers found in captured requests and responses, including URLs, GraphQL doc_id values, object IDs, and operations.

Meta Zurp AI Toolkit

In practical terms, this can reduce the time needed to identify what an unfamiliar value represents when reviewing a large volume of Facebook, Instagram, or other Meta service traffic.

Zurp includes Meta Context, FBDL, CSRF handling, and SPARTA. Meta Context explains identifiers in a request. FBDL helps researchers create and manage test accounts and assets that are allowed for use in Meta’s testing environment.

SPARTA provides leads that may help researchers identify areas needing closer review, then queues proof-of-concept work into Burp Suite Organizer.

According to documentation in the Zurp GitHub repository, each capability can be used separately, although they can also work together in a single research workflow.

One of the more useful Burp Suite features is automated handling of anti-CSRF values. Security researchers often capture a valid request, move it into Burp Repeater, and find that it fails because short-lived values have changed.

Zurp can collect values such as fb_dtsg, lsd, and CSRF tokens from browsing traffic, then replace supported placeholders before a request is sent.

This may make authorized replay testing more stable while keeping values separated by host and logged-in account. The toolkit also supports an AI-assisted path through three separate MCP servers: meta-context, fbdl, and sparta.

A compatible MCP client, such as Claude Code or Muse Code, can use those services to inspect a captured request, identify known Meta values, or work with authorized test assets. The approach reflects a wider move toward human-led AI support in application security testing.

Cyber Security News recently covered AI-powered Burp Suite extensibility, where AI functions are being added around established testing workflows rather than replacing researcher review.

Researchers can install the prebuilt zurp.jar extension in Burp Suite through the Extensions menu, then add a Meta researcher token in Zurp settings.

The project requires Burp Suite 2024.7 or later. Building the extension from source requires Java 17, while the agent-side MCP services require Node.js 22.19.0 or newer.

Access remains restricted. Zurp uses the same allowlist model as Meta’s FBDL service, and users without eligible access receive HTTP 403 responses. According to the project documentation, tokens last 60 days.

Researchers should generate tokens while signed in to the correct enrolled bug bounty account, since a token created under another account can fail authorization checks.

The project is notable because it connects manual proxy-based testing, authorized test data, and AI agent workflows without removing the human researcher from the process.

Meta’s bug bounty program paid more than $2.3 million to researchers during 2024, with roughly 600 valid reports receiving rewards from nearly 10,000 submissions. For broader context on how Burp Suite supports web testing, readers can also review Cyber Security News’ guide to web security scanners.

Researchers can access the source code and installation guidance through the Zurp GitHub repository, while Meta’s FBDL eligibility criteria outline who may use the approved testing environment.

articles.title: Amazon Fire TV Cube 3 Exploit Enables Root Access and Bootloader Unlock
articles.description:
A public exploit package now lets owners of Amazon’s third-generation Fire TV Cube gain persistent root access and unlock the bootloader on firmware PS7717 or older. Released by XDA developer Pro-me3us, the project targets devices known as “gazelle”. It combines temporary root access with a separate bootloader flaw to enable deeper system changes. According to […]

The post Amazon Fire TV Cube 3 Exploit Enables Root Access and Bootloader Unlock appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A public exploit package now lets owners of Amazon’s third-generation Fire TV Cube gain persistent root access and unlock the bootloader on firmware PS7717 or older.

Released by XDA developer Pro-me3us, the project targets devices known as “gazelle”. It combines temporary root access with a separate bootloader flaw to enable deeper system changes.

According to the XDA development thread, the unlock installs Magisk and TWRP recovery, opens restricted boot options, and supports alternative operating systems.

However, the developer warns that the process can permanently damage the device. It also performs an automatic factory reset and requires 1.5GB of user storage to maintain the unlock.

The process starts through Android Debug Bridge, or ADB, with debugging enabled and a connection authorized on the Cube. A temporary root tool gives the unlock script the permissions it needs. The device then restarts into TWRP to complete the changes before returning to FireOS for setup.

Amazon Fire TV Cube 3 Exploit

The project credits mforce2 with porting the Ghostlock exploit, associated with CVE-2026-43499, and NebuSec with developing the original exploit chain. John Red is credited with finding the bootloader vulnerability, while Pro-me3us brought the components together.

The thread also credits researcher Man Yue Mo’s earlier Mali GPU work involving CVE-2022-38181 and CVE-2022-46395 as a basis for testing and information gathering. These are separate contributions, not evidence that every listed flaw runs during each unlock.

Cybersecurity News previously covered how vulnerabilities in the Mali GPU driver can enable device takeover. That reporting explains the broader risk of low-level driver bugs, though it concerns different vulnerabilities than those credited here.

Once unlocked, the Cube gains Magisk support, TWRP backup and recovery features, unrestricted fastboot, and Amlogic download mode. Owners can also access the U-Boot command line over Ethernet and boot from USB storage.

The changes allow custom launchers, modified system and vendor partitions, and custom kernels or ROMs. Related projects include CoreELEC for Kodi-based media playback and EmuELEC for retro gaming. These features turn the streaming device into a more flexible platform for testing and personal use.

Version 1.2, dated September 30, 2026, extends the temporary root tool to PS7717/5741, updates Magisk to version 30.7, and includes a local ADB fix. It also clears the misc partition during unlocking to address firmware updates downloaded before the process begins.

The published method requires enabled, authorized ADB access. It is not presented as an unauthenticated remote attack, and the supplied thread does not report malicious exploitation in the wild.

The developer warns users never to modify the logo partition, which maintains the unlock, or rerun the bootloader unlock script. Running the temporary root tool twice within one boot can also crash and restart the Cube.

The package turns off automatic firmware updates, creating a security tradeoff for owners who keep the unlock. Related Samsung boot-chain research shows why control below Android can have lasting security effects, though those flaws are unrelated.

For everyday users, preserving normal updates remains the safer choice. Researchers should back up data, confirm the exact model and firmware, and weigh the risk of permanent damage before proceeding.

articles.description:
Progress released urgent security updates for MarkLogic Server to fix a broad set of critical and high-severity flaws that could let attackers gain elevated access, create unauthorized administrator accounts, execute code on servers, steal credentials, and access protected data. The security alert, published on October 12, 2026, affects MarkLogic Server 12.0 through 12.0.3 and MarkLogic […]

The post Critical Progress MarkLogic Flaws Enable Remote Code Execution and Admin Takeover appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Progress released urgent security updates for MarkLogic Server to fix a broad set of critical and high-severity flaws that could let attackers gain elevated access, create unauthorized administrator accounts, execute code on servers, steal credentials, and access protected data.

The security alert, published on October 12, 2026, affects MarkLogic Server 12.0 through 12.0.3 and MarkLogic Server 11.0 through 11.3.6.

Progress has released MarkLogic Server 12.1 and 11.3.7 to address the issues. Organizations running retired MarkLogic versions, including version 10 and earlier, should move to a supported fixed release because those versions were not fully assessed and will not receive fixes.

The most serious MarkLogic flaws involve improper privilege management, where a user with limited access may be able to perform actions reserved for an administrator.

CVE-2026-85947 affects forest-management operations and could let a remote user with forest-management permissions create a persistent, unauthorized administrator account.

Progress MarkLogic Flaws

Another issue, CVE-2026-85948, is an XQuery injection flaw in a deprecated Management API package path. A remote user with manage-user-level permissions could use the flaw to gain persistent administrative control. These weaknesses matter because a low-level account can become a long-term entry point into the database platform.

CVE-2026-85955 may allow a user with query-execution access to invoke an XQuery evaluation function without the required extra privilege. Progress said this could result in server-side code execution with elevated permissions.

CVE-2026-85960 also creates a code execution path through predictable cross-site request forgery tokens in Query Console. A malicious webpage could send unauthorized requests when opened by an authenticated Query Console user, causing server-side code to run with that user’s permissions.

This pattern resembles other recent Progress product security issues, including the Progress OpenEdge AdminServer flaw that allowed authenticated users to inject operating-system commands through remote administration features.

Cyber Security News has also reported on Progress ShareFile vulnerabilities that could be chained to obtain remote code execution on affected customer-managed deployments.

Several vulnerabilities could expose cloud services and authentication material. CVE-2026-85951 affects Azure-based installations and could enable server-side request forgery, or SSRF, allowing an authenticated user to request internal cloud services and potentially obtain credentials or tokens. CVE-2026-85952 presents a similar risk on Linux systems.

Progress also fixed CVE-2026-85962, an improper SAML authentication issue. In deployments that use SAML, an unauthenticated remote attacker could cause MarkLogic to accept an assertion that should have been rejected, opening a path to unauthorized access.

Other notable issues include XML external entity processing flaws, path traversal weaknesses, sensitive data written to logs, unsafe TLS certificate hostname validation, and cleartext transport for certain cluster-management and Amazon S3 connections.

The bulletin also lists memory-safety flaws that could cause process crashes, limited memory disclosure, or data modification. Progress strongly recommends upgrading MarkLogic Server 12.0–12.0.3 to version 12.1 and upgrading the 11.x branch through 11.3.6 to version 11.3.7. The vendor says Progress Data Cloud customers have already been patched.

Administrators should review administrator accounts, forest-management permissions, Query Console access, REST and XDBC evaluation paths, authentication events, diagnostic logs, and unexpected outbound connections.

The company warned that affected servers may operate normally and that missing indicators do not prove a system has not been compromised.

Before upgrading, teams should back up content and security databases. Progress notes that MarkLogic Server does not support downgrades, so an upgrade cannot simply be reversed after installation. Older MarkLogic Content Pump clients should also be upgraded to versions that match MarkLogic Server 12.1 or 11.3.7.

The large number of fixed flaws makes this more than a routine patch cycle. Organizations should prioritize exposed management interfaces, privileged MarkLogic users, cloud-connected deployments, and SAML-enabled environments when applying the vendor’s updates.

articles.title: Critical MariaDB Flaws Can Let Attackers Execute Code and Steal Database Data

The post Critical MariaDB Flaws Can Let Attackers Execute Code and Steal Database Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
MariaDB has disclosed security flaws that, under specific conditions, could let attackers run code, access restricted database tables, and steal login credentials.

The issues affect several server branches and MariaDB Connector/C. Although the headline describes a critical risk, the vendor rates the main code execution flaws as High, not Critical. Exploitation depends on installed plugins, account permissions, or unsafe settings.

The leading concern is CVE-2026-107815, a memory corruption flaw in the CONNECT storage engine. MariaDB assigns it a CVSS score of 8.5 and says researchers demonstrated remote code execution in laboratory conditions.

The advisory describes a network attack requiring low privileges, high attack complexity, and no user interaction. It does not report confirmed attacks against live systems.

The CONNECT flaw affects how it handles its DOS table. A faulty boundary check allows an attacker to write one zero byte beyond a stack buffer at an attacker-controlled position.

Even this small write can corrupt memory in a way that supports code execution, as the laboratory test showed. MariaDB recommends removing the CONNECT engine plugin when you don’t need it.

Critical MariaDB Vulnerability

A second issue, CVE-2026-107821, affects checks on binary .frm files that MariaDB reads when opening tables. Specially crafted files can cause crashes, out-of-bounds reads or writes, and potentially remote code execution. The official MariaDB advisory rates this vulnerability High with a CVSS score of 8.0.

That attack has important limits. Placing a malicious file in the database directory requires the FILE privilege and a secure-file-priv setting that permits access there.

MariaDB says properly configured servers block file-level access to this directory and grant FILE sparingly. These requirements make it misleading to describe the flaw as an unrestricted attack against every exposed server.

The separate CVE-2026-102523 vulnerability could allow attackers to read or change tables outside their normal permissions. MariaDB failed to encode partition names safely for filesystem use during ALTER TABLE … CONVERT … PARTITION operations. Its partition security advisory gives the issue a CVSS score of 8.0. It lists low privileges and user interaction as attack requirements.

Connector/C also needs attention. CVE-2026-107819 affects libmariadb versions 3.4.1 through 3.4.9. An attacker positioned between client and server could present a valid certificate for the wrong host and request cleartext password authentication.

A programming mistake could allow the client to send its password over that unverified connection. Other MariaDB connectors are not affected. The risks extend beyond server code alone.

Cybersecuritynews previously covered a cPanel database privilege flaw involving MySQL and MariaDB access, along with a PostgreSQL tool injection flaw that could enable code execution. Those separate reports provide useful context on how database permissions and supporting tools can widen an attack’s impact.

The CONNECT and binary .frm flaws affect MariaDB 10.6.1–10.6.27, 10.11.1–10.11.18, 11.4.1–11.4.12, 11.8.1–11.8.8, 12.3.1–12.3.2, and 13.0.1. Fixes are available in 10.6.28, 10.11.19, 11.4.13, 11.8.9, 12.3.3, and 13.0.2. The partition flaw does not list the 10.6 branch as affected.

Administrators should upgrade affected server branches and update Connector/C to 3.4.10. While preparing updates, remove unused CONNECT plugins and review FILE permissions and database-directory access.

MariaDB also offers disabling partition support as a workaround for the partition flaw. Apply that measure only after checking whether existing databases depend on partitioned tables.

articles.title: GhostProfile macOS Malware Clones Browser Profiles to Hijack Live Sessions
articles.description:
A newly reported macOS malware called GhostProfile clones browser profiles and lets attackers control hidden copies of Chrome or Firefox using the victim’s active logins. Rather than showing or copying the visible desktop, the malware creates a separate browser workspace where an operator can browse websites with cookies taken from the infected Mac. The threat […]

The post GhostProfile macOS Malware Clones Browser Profiles to Hijack Live Sessions appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A newly reported macOS malware called GhostProfile clones browser profiles and lets attackers control hidden copies of Chrome or Firefox using the victim’s active logins.

Rather than showing or copying the visible desktop, the malware creates a separate browser workspace where an operator can browse websites with cookies taken from the infected Mac.

The threat moves beyond collecting passwords for later use. By working inside a copied browser profile, an attacker may reach accounts whose sessions remain valid without another sign-in.

The victim’s normal browser can remain open while activity takes place elsewhere, making account misuse harder to notice through visible screen changes alone.

Researchers from Moonlock Lab identified the malware after receiving a sample shared by MalwareHunterTeam and disclosed their findings on October 12, 2026.

In its initial GhostProfile research thread, the team described the sample as apparently undetected at that point. That early observation does not establish universal antivirus evasion, and the researchers noted that the delivery script was already detectable.

GhostProfile macOS Malware Clones Browser Profiles

Traditional hidden Virtual Network Computing, or hVNC, malware usually creates a concealed desktop. GhostProfile instead builds a temporary browser-profile clone and controls it through Chrome DevTools Protocol, known as CDP, and WebDriver BiDi.

These browser interfaces give the operator a way to interact with pages while using the copied login state. The approach resembles techniques covered in AmnesiaStealer hidden browser control, where a second-stage component copies browser profiles and operates a concealed Chromium session.

The shared concern is live account access rather than password theft alone. However, similar behavior does not establish that GhostProfile and AmnesiaStealer share developers, infrastructure, or an underlying codebase.

To conceal its browser window, GhostProfile moves it to screen coordinates far outside the visible display. It also changes the browser’s automation flag and spoofs WebGL and plugin information.

These changes appear intended to make automated browsing less obvious to websites, although Moonlock’s disclosure does not demonstrate that every site accepts the disguise.

The operator receives JPEG screenshots and can send simulated mouse clicks and keyboard input. Moonlock also reported that the implant grants its controlled browser permissions for camera, microphone, location, notifications, and clipboard access.

Those capabilities widen the potential impact, but the disclosure does not show that operators used every permission against victims.

Delivery, Persistence, and Data Theft

The infection chain begins with a short shell command that passes downloaded content into the zsh shell. Its delivery script fetches the agent, removes its quarantine marker, places the payload in the Downloads folder, and registers a fake system-updater LaunchAgent. RunAtLoad and KeepAlive settings support automatic startup and continued operation.

This disguise follows a familiar pattern in fake updater persistence attacks, where malware borrows trusted software names to hide startup entries.

GhostProfile’s reported updater identity should therefore be checked against its file location and behavior, rather than accepted as legitimate simply because the name sounds like a system component.

GhostProfile focuses on Chromium-family browsers and Firefox, the browser types it can control. It examines cookie stores using SQLite tools and reads the system clipboard through the macOS NSPasteboard interface.

The agent also contains a readable hVNC banner, a default pre-shared key, and temporary working directories that it removes on exit.

An additional upload-and-run function makes the implant a loader. An operator can send a ZIP archive or disk image, after which the agent extracts or mounts it, finds an application, clears quarantine, and launches it.

This creates a route for additional payloads, although Moonlock did not identify a confirmed follow-on malware family. The broader risk matches Odyssey Stealer browser theft, where stolen cookies can expose accounts without immediately revealing their passwords.

GhostProfile adds direct interaction with a concealed browser. Still, its reported cloning capability should not be treated as proof that every session remains usable or that all additional authentication checks can be bypassed.

Security teams should investigate unexpected browser-profile copies, hidden browser launches, unfamiliar updater LaunchAgents, and connections to the reported infrastructure.

Suspected Macs should be isolated while evidence is preserved. Account recovery should include revoking exposed sessions and changing credentials from a trusted device, rather than relying on a password reset alone to end ongoing access.

articles.title: Kimsuky Operation GitPower Uses GitHub to Deliver Malware and Steal Data
articles.description:
Kimsuky is using GitHub and other trusted code platforms to deliver malware, run commands, and steal data from Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security, and international policy. The North Korea-linked group’s Operation GitPower combines targeted emails, fake PDF files, and Windows scripts to turn routine work requests into possible entry points for cyber spying. The attacks […]

The post Kimsuky Operation GitPower Uses GitHub to Deliver Malware and Steal Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Kimsuky is using GitHub and other trusted code platforms to deliver malware, run commands, and steal data from Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security, and international policy.

The North Korea-linked group’s Operation GitPower combines targeted emails, fake PDF files, and Windows scripts to turn routine work requests into possible entry points for cyber spying.

The attacks use conference invitations and research requests to build trust before sending harmful files. Codeberg hosts malicious archives, GitLab supplies decoy documents and scripts, and GitHub supports payload delivery and data transfers.

Most observed attempts against the Ukrainian targets were unsuccessful, an important limit on the campaign’s reported impact.

Researchers from Genians identified the activity in an October 12, 2026 report, linking it to earlier Operation GitPower attacks through shared code, file names, scheduled tasks, and methods used to upload stolen information. Their findings show how the group changes its email themes while keeping much of its attack framework.

Kimsuky Operation GitPower

One attack began on August 6 with a fake speaking invitation to the Korea Cyber Security Conference. The email used real event details, praised the recipient’s work, and offered travel support and payment.

Unlike earlier Kimsuky GitHub attacks that delivered malicious shortcuts, this case started with a message containing no harmful link or attachment.

Only after a target replied did the attacker send a ZIP archive with invitation materials. A later version used password protection, which researchers assessed as an effort to make inspection harder for email security tools.

Inside, a genuine-looking HTML invitation helped hide a Windows shortcut dressed up as a PDF. A separate approach on August 19 impersonated a policy researcher seeking feedback on a report about Russia and North Korea.

After receiving a reply, the attacker sent a Codeberg download link. When the malware attempt failed, a September follow-up switched to a fake meeting login page designed to steal account details.

Opening the malicious shortcut starts cmd.exe and uses curl to download files from GitLab. Depending on the version, a decoy PDF opens while another download is saved as a VBE script and runs in the background. The initial script retrieves a follow-up component that executes in memory.

The loader hides PowerShell commands by inserting extra words, then removes them with Replace() just before execution.

The follow-up script creates a task that looks like a Google update and runs every 15 minutes. It collects systeminfo output and a listing of the user’s Downloads folder, rather than automatically stealing every file there.

GitHub Malware Delivery and Data Theft

Collected information is encoded in Base64 and uploaded through the GitHub Contents API using a hardcoded access token. Temporary files and the initial script are then deleted.

Similar use of GitHub and recurring tasks appeared in Kimsuky AI phishing campaigns covered previously, although those earlier findings included AsyncRAT payloads not established for this Ukrainian attack chain.

Other September samples used peace-report and researcher résumé themes. Their shortcuts downloaded files named LICENSE and okay.md from GitHub, but these contained VBScript and PowerShell code.

A OneDrive-themed task ran every minute, allowing a separate control server to deliver more scripts and receive files created during their execution.

The group also placed an unsigned, 64-bit fake Zoom installer in a public GitHub repository. It drops hidden scripts, creates a task that runs every minute, and contacts the same control server used by the September shortcut samples.

It then downloads and starts the real Zoom installer, giving users a familiar installation screen after malware is already present.

The wider operation has also featured Kimsuky OpenCode phishing decoys in earlier research, showing how lure production can change without replacing the core script-based approach.

Genians linked the Ukrainian activity to Kimsuky through combined technical evidence, not simply the use of GitHub or the subject of an email.

Genians assesses that the targeting may support spying on the war and ongoing cooperation between South Korea and Ukraine.

Japanese decoy documents found in related repositories also suggest possible interest in Japanese speakers, but do not confirm successful attacks. The report does not establish that every file stored in those repositories reached an intended victim.

For defenders, the report recommends linking endpoint events rather than blocking every development platform. A shortcut launching cmd.exe, curl, or hidden PowerShell should be reviewed alongside new scripts, update-themed tasks, GitHub API uploads, and unusual network connections.

Installer checks should include digital signatures and background activity, since a real setup screen does not prove that the file launching it is safe.

articles.title: Critical SonicWall Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks Following Disclosure
articles.description:
A critical SonicWall SMA1000 flaw, CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS 10.0), is being actively exploited days after disclosure, allowing unauthenticated attackers to make vulnerable appliances send requests on their behalf. Threat intelligence firms detected exploitation attempts beginning October 8, two days after SonicWall released fixes. The activity affects SonicWall Secure Mobile Access appliances used to provide remote access […]

The post Critical SonicWall Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks Following Disclosure appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical SonicWall SMA1000 flaw, CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS 10.0), is being actively exploited days after disclosure, allowing unauthenticated attackers to make vulnerable appliances send requests on their behalf.

Threat intelligence firms detected exploitation attempts beginning October 8, two days after SonicWall released fixes. The activity affects SonicWall Secure Mobile Access appliances used to provide remote access to business resources.

Defused Cyber reported suspicious traffic against its SMA decoys, while Previdian detected attempts consistent with the same vulnerability.

These findings show attackers are targeting the flaw, although the available reports do not establish successful breaches of customer networks.

The flaw is a server-side request forgery, or SSRF, issue in the SMA1000 Work Place interface. An unintended alternate access path allows a remote attacker to use the appliance as a proxy.

Instead of sending requests directly to protected services, the attacker makes the trusted appliance send them, potentially reaching internal functions and carrying out unauthorized operations.

The lack of a login requirement makes this vulnerability especially serious. Attackers don’t need a stolen account or user interaction to exploit it.

SonicWall assigned the flaw a critical rating because it could impact on data confidentiality, system integrity, and service availability. Its product notice urges affected customers to install the latest hotfix.

Critical SonicWall Vulnerability Exploited

SonicWall disclosed the vulnerabilities on October 6, 2026. Its notice stated that there was no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Later observations changed the picture, with Defused and Previdian reporting attempts against their monitoring systems. Defused Cyber said the first traffic reached its decoys on October 8, showing how quickly attackers moved after disclosure.

According to The Hacker News, Previdian recorded 135 attempts from two IP addresses located in the United States. Those figures describe activity seen by its sensors, not the number of compromised organizations. The IP addresses’ locations also do not indicate where the attackers were based.

The same release addresses three additional flaws. CVE-2026-102256 involves command injection that can allow code execution after authentication.

CVE-2026-102257 is a Zip Slip issue that can write extracted files outside their intended directory. CVE-2026-102258 allows stored JavaScript to run in the Appliance Management Console. These issues require authenticated access, unlike the critical SSRF flaw.

Earlier SonicWall zero-day attacks used separate SSRF and command injection vulnerabilities to gain root access and deploy custom malware. Cybersecurity News also covered SMA1000 remote code execution attacks in September. Those reports provide relevant background, but they do not prove the current attempts involve the same attackers or techniques.

Affected devices include SMA1000 models 6210, 7210, and 8200v running 12.4.3-03526 or older, or 12.5.0-02952 or older. Administrators should upgrade to 12.4.3-03670 or later, or 12.5.0-03082 or later, using the appropriate software branch. SonicWall lists no workaround.

The advisory excludes the SMA 100 product line and SSL-VPN services on SonicWall firewalls. Administrators should confirm their exact appliance model and installed hotfix rather than assume every SonicWall VPN product is affected. With exploitation attempts already reported, affected deployments warrant urgent patching.

The outage lasted four hours and 12 minutes, according to OMG! Ubuntu. It was Canonical’s second major DDoS incident this year, following a broader disruption in late April. Canonical confirmed the […]

The post Massive DDoS Attack Disrupts Ubuntu’s Canonical Websites and Security APIs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu Linux, suffered a sustained distributed denial-of-service attack on October 8, 2026, disrupting its main websites and security information services. The outage lasted four hours and 12 minutes, according to OMG! Ubuntu. It was Canonical’s second major DDoS incident this year, following a broader disruption in late April.

Canonical confirmed the incident through Ubuntu Discourse, warning that some services could become intermittently unavailable. “Canonical’s websites are under a sustained distributed denial of service attack,” the company stated. Its engineers worked to restore access, and an October 9 update said most affected services were available again while recovery work continued.

Ubuntu Websites and Security APIs Affected

The affected services included ubuntu.com, canonical.com, the Ubuntu blog, the developer portal, and Ubuntu’s security advisory pages and API. These resources provide product information, developer guidance, and vulnerability details. Their disruption left users unable to reliably reach parts of Ubuntu’s public web infrastructure, even though several software delivery services continued operating.

The security API outage was particularly relevant to administrators and automated tools that retrieve vulnerability records and security notices. When those endpoints are unavailable, checks may fail or receive information later than expected. However, the reported interruption does not establish that security records were changed, software packages were compromised, or attackers accessed customer systems.

Launchpad, the Snap Store, Ubuntu Single Sign-On, personal package archives, and the CD image server remained operational during the October incident, according to OMG! Ubuntu’s report. Package repositories were also unaffected. This limited the disruption, allowing software downloads and package operations to continue despite problems reaching the main websites and security pages.

Canonical has not publicly disclosed the attack’s traffic volume, technical method, or origin. No group appeared to have claimed responsibility in reporting published on October 12. Although the outage affected prominent services, there is no published bandwidth figure supporting a measured description of its scale. The confirmed impact was a sustained loss of availability.

The earlier incident reached more services, including Launchpad and the Snap Store. Cybersecurity News covered that event in its report on the Ubuntu website and Canonical DDoS attack.

For Ubuntu users, the incident highlights the need to distinguish website outages from package delivery failures. Administrators should track Canonical’s official status page before assuming every Ubuntu service is affected.

articles.title: Yandex Data Center Outage Disrupts Access to Cloud Files Following Drone Attack
articles.description:
Yandex has confirmed a major service outage after drone attacks damaged three data centers in Russia, leaving some users unable to access cloud files. Two facilities stopped operating, while a third lost part of its infrastructure. The disruption affected Yandex Disk users and businesses running services on Yandex Cloud across the platform. The first attack […]

The post Yandex Data Center Outage Disrupts Access to Cloud Files Following Drone Attack appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Yandex has confirmed a major service outage after drone attacks damaged three data centers in Russia, leaving some users unable to access cloud files. Two facilities stopped operating, while a third lost part of its infrastructure. The disruption affected Yandex Disk users and businesses running services on Yandex Cloud across the platform.

The first attack hit the Sasovo data center during the night of October 7 to 8, 2026. Yandex said the site suffered serious damage and stopped operating completely. Another attack struck its Kaluga facility on October 9, disabling part of the infrastructure. A third attack hit Vladimir overnight on October 11 and halted operations there.

Yandex reported no injuries across the three incidents. Emergency teams and company specialists were working at the damaged sites. In its statement, the company said engineers were working day and night to keep services running, but assessing the equipment remained difficult. It could not provide a reliable restoration timeline.

Cloud Files Become Unavailable

The outage has exposed problems beyond simply opening an application. That one Yandex Disk customer experienced missing thumbnails and failed downloads of previously uploaded files, with problems beginning on October 8. The customer also reported HTTP 302 redirects, HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout errors, and HTTP 500 errors while accessing files.

These reports show that some stored content could not be retrieved through normal service requests. However, failed downloads do not establish that files have been deleted. Whether any customer data has been permanently lost remains unclear, and Yandex had not addressed that question in the status updates cited by BleepingComputer.

The impact also extended to business cloud tools. The report said Yandex Cloud’s console, API, identity management, container registry, databases, S3 storage, and Kubernetes were available with some performance or availability issues. Compute, AI Studio, and security services were only partly available, while Monium remained offline. Those conditions reflected the latest update cited in the October 12 report, not a guarantee of current availability.

Yandex described its remaining cloud resources as unstable and said the platform was operating in emergency mode. It urged customers to use alternative disaster recovery plans and warned that technical support channels could also be unstable.

The incident concerns physical damage to hosting infrastructure. The available reporting does not establish a malware infection, stolen credentials, or unauthorized access to customer files.

Related coverage of a Microsoft data center power outage and the AWS outage linked to DNS problems shows how infrastructure failures can interrupt services far beyond the original fault.

For affected organizations, Yandex’s warning makes recovery planning urgent. Access to another working environment matters while damaged facilities remain offline. The immediate unanswered questions are when full service will return and whether all affected files can be recovered.

articles.title: WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks to Upload and eEecute Arbitrary PHP code
articles.description:
Attackers are targeting a critical security flaw in the Bricksforge WordPress plugin that lets them upload and run arbitrary PHP code without logging in. Tracked as CVE-2026-85097, the vulnerability carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and can lead to remote code execution on affected websites. Patchstack first observed exploitation attempts on October 7, 2026, […]

The post WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks to Upload and eEecute Arbitrary PHP code appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are targeting a critical security flaw in the Bricksforge WordPress plugin that lets them upload and run arbitrary PHP code without logging in.

Tracked as CVE-2026-85097, the vulnerability carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and can lead to remote code execution on affected websites. Patchstack first observed exploitation attempts on October 7, 2026, at 21:47:17 UTC.

The flaw affects Bricksforge versions up to and including 3.1.8.9. Patchstack identifies version 3.1.8.10 as the fixed release. Bricksforge extends Bricks Builder with advanced forms, animations, dynamic data tools, and site controls. Its form upload process is at the center of this attack.

According to Patchstack’s technical report, Bricksforge checks a file’s MIME type during the initial upload. This check helps identify whether the submitted file is an allowed image. However, when a form is submitted later, the plugin trusts the visitor-supplied file details without properly checking the URL field inside temporaryFileUploads.

Attackers exploit this gap by uploading a file that looks like a GIF but also contains PHP code. The image passes the first check and enters the temporary upload directory. A crafted form submission then pairs the image’s server path with a destination URL ending in a PHP extension.

Bricksforge accepts those details and places the file contents at the PHP destination. Requesting that file causes the server to execute the hidden code.

Attackers can then install web shells, change website content, read sensitive data, or maintain access. The attack also uses the publicly accessible bricksforge_regenerate_nonce AJAX action to obtain a valid request token.

WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Exploited

This is separate from the earlier Bricks Builder remote code execution vulnerability. It also highlights risks seen in other WordPress plugin file upload flaws, where unsafe file handling can turn an upload feature into a code execution path.

Almost every captured attempt targeted /wp-json/bricksforge/v1/form_submit. One used /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php with the bricksforge_form_submit action. In 95% of requests, the server path ended in .gif or .png, often paired with a PHP destination URL.

Attackers tested extensions including .php5, .php8, and .phtml, alongside mixed capitalization and encoded filenames. Some attempted to place login_admin_*.php files outside the temporary directory, in regular WordPress upload folders.

Patchstack recorded 63 source IP addresses. One cluster involved 44 IPs sending 56 identical requests within seconds. Another involved three IPs testing 25 extension and encoding variations. These patterns suggest automated activity using distributed infrastructure, but they do not establish a single attacker’s identity.

Administrators should update affected installations to version 3.1.8.10 or later. The vendor changelog also lists a Pro Forms upload security fix in version 4.0.1, released October 8, and urges updates even when active forms have no upload fields.

Review logs for crafted temporaryFileUploads submissions and inspect /wp-content/uploads/bricksforge/tmp/ and other upload directories for unexpected PHP files. Check for requests to newly created scripts and unauthorized changes.

Patchstack says its RapidMitigate rule blocks exploitation attempts, offering temporary protection when immediate updates are not possible. Sites previously exposed should still undergo a compromise review.

articles.title: LG webOS Flaws Let Remote Attackers Execute Commands as Root Without Authentication
articles.description:

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2023-6317 through CVE-2023-6320, affect selected LG TV models running webOS versions 4 through 7. Bitdefender researchers said the issue could […]

The post LG webOS Flaws Let Remote Attackers Execute Commands as Root Without Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security researchers have disclosed four serious vulnerabilities in LG webOS smart TVs that could allow an attacker to bypass authentication, create a privileged account, and ultimately execute commands with root-level access.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2023-6317 through CVE-2023-6320, affect selected LG TV models running webOS versions 4 through 7.

Bitdefender researchers said the issue could give an attacker full control of a vulnerable television if it is reachable on the same local network.

In some cases, the risk could extend beyond the home network because researchers found more than 91,000 exposed devices through Shodan. This search engine indexes internet-connected services. Bitdefender said LG fixed the reported issues before it publicly released the research in April 2024.

The most important flaw, CVE-2023-6317, affects the pairing process used by the LG ThinQ mobile app. Normally, when setting up the app, a user must enter a PIN displayed on the TV before the app can gain access.

LG webOS Flaws

Bitdefender found that a weakness in the webOS account-registration process could let an attacker skip that PIN verification and create a user profile with elevated permissions.

The problem involved how the system handled client-key and companion-client-key values. An attacker could first request a low-permission account, obtain its client key, and then reuse that key while requesting another account with higher permissions.

The TV verified that the key existed but did not properly confirm that it belonged to the account being created. That allowed the request to avoid the on-screen PIN prompt.

Once the attacker created a privileged account, they could access services unavailable to normal unauthenticated users. This is where the remaining flaws become important.

CVE-2023-6318 and CVE-2023-6319 are command-injection vulnerabilities that can be used to run operating system commands. CVE-2023-6320 affects a network configuration endpoint and can run commands under the dbus account, which researchers said has permissions close to root.

For readers following smart-TV security issues, Cyber Security News previously reported that more than 90,000 LG TVs were exposed to authorization bypass risks, highlighting how internet exposure can turn a local-network weakness into a wider concern.

Bitdefender confirmed the flaws on several webOS builds, including webOS 4.9.7, 5.5.0, 6.3.3-442, and 7.3.1-43. The tested devices included the LG43UM7000PLA, OLED55CXPUA, OLED48C1PUB, and OLED55A23LA.

CVE-2023-6317 affected all four tested webOS versions and enabled the authentication bypass. CVE-2023-6318 was confirmed on webOS 5.5.0, 6.3.3-442, and 7.3.1-43. CVE-2023-6319 affected all tested versions, while CVE-2023-6320 affected webOS 5.5.0 and 6.3.3-442.

The full chain is particularly concerning because it combines a simple authorization bypass with command execution. A threat actor would not need a TV owner to approve a pairing request or enter a PIN.

After obtaining elevated access, they could change settings, install unwanted software, access connected services, or use the TV as a foothold inside a home network.

LG’s Product Security Response Center publishes security bulletins for product issues, and the company says smart TVs receive software and security updates at least once a year for at least two years after launch. LG also says its security update period lasts five years from the webOS platform launch date.

Owners should turn on automatic software updates and manually check the TV’s firmware version through the device settings. Updating is especially important after unboxing a TV that may have sat in storage for months before you connect it to the internet.

Users should also avoid exposing smart TVs directly to the internet through router port forwarding, keep home routers patched, and, where possible, place IoT devices on a separate guest or IoT network. These steps reduce the chance that an outside attacker can reach a vulnerable TV or use it to move deeper into a home network.
